title: When the assumptions fail
objectives: Check residuals for changing variance and autocorrelation, and use robust errors.

screens.title: A funnel
screens.prose: A broker fits execution cost against order size for twelve orders. The line is the least squares fit, $\hat y = 1.86 + 0.539x$, and each stick is a residual.
screens.question: Tap the three orders the line misses by the most.

hints.text: Look at the length of each residual stick, up or down.
The long sticks are all on one side of the chart.
The orders of £9m, £11m and £12m miss by 1.44, 0.72 and 1.10.

feedback.correct: The three biggest misses are all large orders.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the residual sticks, ignoring their sign.

byKey.p0: That £1m order sits almost on the line. Look further right.
byKey.p5: The £6m order misses by 0.39; three large orders miss by more.
byKey.p9: The £10m order misses by 0.44. The £11m order misses by 0.72.

explain.text: Small orders hug the line; large ones scatter widely. The spread of the residuals grows with $x$, a funnel. Constant variance, an assumption behind the usual standard errors, fails here.

screens.title: Does today echo yesterday?
screens.prose: These are the residuals of a daily regression over 41 days. Each dot plots one day's residual against the day before. If the days were independent, the cloud would have no tilt.
screens.question: Tilt the line to follow the cloud. Roughly what slope fits?

widget.label: Slope of today on yesterday
widget.accept: Anything from 0.60 to 0.84. The least squares slope is 0.72.

hints.text: Slide the slope until the line runs through the middle of the cloud.
Most dots sit in the bottom-left and top-right corners.
The cloud rises about 0.7 for each 1 along the axis.

feedback.correct: About 0.72: a large residual today predicts a large one tomorrow.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tilt the line until it splits the cloud evenly.

byKey.flat: A flat line would mean no echo. The dots cluster in the bottom-left and top-right, so the slope is positive.
byKey.neg: A negative slope would mean residuals flip sign each day. Here they keep their sign.

explain.text: The least squares slope is 0.72: residuals persist from day to day. That is **autocorrelation**, and it breaks the independence assumption. Its usual summary is the Durbin-Watson statistic, here 0.58.

screens.title: What the funnel breaks
screens.prose: We simulated 10,000 samples of 100 days from a funnel model with true slope 1.2. Each bar is measured across the 10,000 fits. The average slope came out at 1.200.

state.caption: Usual 95% intervals covered the truth 80% of the time; robust ones 94%.

screens.question: What has the funnel broken?

options.text: The usual standard error: it is far too small
The slope: it is biased
options.why: You blamed the coefficient. Its average over 10,000 fits is 1.200, the true value.

options.text: Both the slope and its standard error
options.why: The slope averages 1.200, so it is fine. Only the spread is misjudged.

options.text: Nothing: the intervals are only a little off
options.why: Missing 20% of the time instead of 5% is four times the promised error rate.

hints.text: Compare the average slope with the true 1.2.
Then compare the usual SE with the actual spread of the slopes.
The slope is right on average, but the usual SE is 0.071 against an actual spread of 0.109.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the average slope, then the bars.

byKey.bias: You blamed the coefficient. A funnel leaves $\hat\beta$ unbiased; it misjudges its spread.

explain.text: Changing variance is **heteroscedasticity**. The slope stays unbiased, but the usual SE assumes one variance for every day and comes out 35% too small. **Robust** (White, or HC) standard errors measure the spread from the residuals themselves: 0.105 against the true 0.109.

screens.title: The Durbin-Watson statistic
screens.prose: The Durbin-Watson statistic compares day-to-day changes in the residuals with their size: $$d = \frac{\sum_{t=2}^{n}(e_t - e_{t-1})^2}{\sum_{t=1}^{n} e_t^2} \approx 2(1 - \hat\rho).$$ Independent residuals give $d$ near 2. Persistent ones give $d$ near 0.
screens.question: Compute $d$ for these eight residuals. The squares of the changes add to 0.55.

hints.text: You need the sum of the squared residuals for the bottom.
The bottom is 1.56, so $d = 0.55/1.56$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 0.55 by the sum of the squared residuals, 1.56.

byKey.inv: You divided the wrong way up. The changes go on top.
byKey.two: 2 is what independent residuals would give. Compute it from these numbers.

explain.text: $d = 0.353$, so $\hat\rho \approx 1 - d/2 = 0.82$. The residuals drift slowly: positive for three days, then negative for five. With $d$ this low, the usual standard errors are too small.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm

def slope_ses(x, y):
    X = sm.add_constant(np.array(x, dtype=float))
    y = np.array(y, dtype=float)
    usual = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()
    hc1 = sm.OLS(y, X).fit(cov_type="HC1")
    hac = sm.OLS(y, X).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 5})
    return [usual.bse[1], hc1.bse[1], hac.bse[1]]
widget.how: Check runs 4 hidden tests on the lists `sig`, `ret`, `mkt` and `stk`, which are already defined. Each result is rounded to 4 places. statsmodels is large: the first run loads NumPy, SciPy, pandas and statsmodels, which takes 15 to 30 seconds.

hints.text: Each robust version is the same `sm.OLS(y, X)` with a different `fit`.
`fit(cov_type="HC1")` gives the White standard errors. The long runs of one sign are what HAC allows for.
`hac = sm.OLS(y, X).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 5})`.

feedback.correct: For `sig` the slope's SE is 0.1115 usual, 0.1047 HC1 and 0.1648 HAC.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. For `sig` and `ret` the answer is `[0.1115, 0.1047, 0.1648]`.

byKey.test-1: For `sig` and `ret` the answer is `[0.1115, 0.1047, 0.1648]`. Check the `cov_type` names and `maxlags`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. `cov_kwds` takes a dictionary: `{"maxlags": 5}`.

explain.text:
For the slow signal, HAC raises the SE from 0.1115 to 0.1648, so $t$ falls from 2.13 to 1.44. For the beta regression `mkt`, `stk`, HC1 raises it from 0.07 to 0.105. The coefficients never change: only their standard errors do.

```python
hac = sm.OLS(y, X).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 5})
```

screens.title: One return per month
screens.prose: A fund's monthly return is regressed on the market's, over 60 months. Each month's return covers its own days, with no overlap. The residuals are below, $d = 1.87$.
screens.question: Do these standard errors need a HAC correction?

options.text: No: with no overlap and $d$ near 2 there is no autocorrelation to correct
Yes: time series always need HAC errors
options.why: You applied HAC by reflex. With separate months and $d$ near 2 it only adds noise to the SE.

options.text: Yes: monthly data are autocorrelated by construction
options.why: That is true of overlapping windows. Separate months share no days.

options.text: No, but switch to log returns first
options.why: Log returns would not change the autocorrelation. Nothing here needs fixing.

hints.text: What makes residuals echo each other?
Overlapping windows share days; separate months do not. The residuals switch sign often.
$d = 1.87$ is close to 2, and no two months share a day.

feedback.correct: Nothing to correct: the usual or HC errors are fine here.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what could link one month's residual to the next.

byKey.always: You applied HAC by reflex. It is a fix for autocorrelation, and these residuals show none.
byKey.monthly: You treated separate months like overlapping windows. Only shared days build in autocorrelation.

explain.text: Non-overlapping returns share no days, and efficient prices make them close to independent. $d = 1.87$ agrees. HAC would cost precision here and fix nothing.

screens.title: A $p$-value of 0.000
screens.prose: A trader regresses a stock's daily implied volatility level on an index's implied volatility level, over 250 days. The summary reports $t = 4.64$ and $p = 0.000$.
screens.question: How much should we trust $p = 0.000$?

options.text: Little: $d = 0.09$ says the residuals are highly persistent, so the SE is far too small
Fully: 250 observations is plenty
options.why: You counted 250 days as 250 independent pieces of news. With $d = 0.09$ each day mostly repeats the last.

options.text: Little, because $R^2$ is only 0.080
options.why: A low $R^2$ does not invalidate a $p$-value. The problem is the Durbin-Watson line.

options.text: Little, because the coefficient is biased
options.why: Autocorrelation leaves $\hat\beta$ unbiased here. It is the standard error that is wrong.

hints.text: One line of the summary checks the independence assumption.
Durbin-Watson near 2 is fine; near 0 is trouble.
With HAC errors over 10 lags the SE rises to 0.116, so $t = 1.69$ and $p = 0.09$.

feedback.correct: With HAC errors the SE is 0.116, $t = 1.69$ and $p = 0.09$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line that checks for autocorrelation.

byKey.lots: You trusted a $p$-value from autocorrelated daily data. Levels like implied volatility drift, so days are far from independent.
byKey.coef: Autocorrelation misleads the standard error, not the coefficient.

explain.text: Implied volatility levels drift slowly, so the residuals do too: $d = 0.092$. The usual SE of 0.042 assumes 250 independent days. HAC errors with 10 lags give 0.116, and the $p$-value rises from 0.000 to 0.09.

screens.title: The assumptions, and what each buys
screens.prose: Least squares assumes: 1. a linear model with errors averaging zero; 2. no perfect collinearity; 3. independent errors; 4. constant variance; 5. normal errors. 1 and 2 make $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ unbiased. 3 and 4 make $\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ right; robust errors replace them. 5 matters only for exact $t$ and $F$ tests in small samples.
screens.question: A beta regression over 2,000 days has fat-tailed residuals that are independent with constant variance. What breaks?

options.text: Very little: with $n = 2{,}000$ the $t$ and $F$ $p$-values are close to right
The $t$-statistics: they need normal errors
options.why: You applied the small-sample rule to a large sample. With 2,000 days the $t$ statistic is close to normal anyway.

options.text: The coefficients: fat tails bias them
options.why: Unbiasedness needs only assumptions 1 and 2.

options.text: The standard errors: switch to HC1
options.why: HC errors fix changing variance. These residuals have constant variance.

hints.text: Which assumption fails here?
Only number 5, normality.
Normality matters only for exact tests in small samples. Here $n = 2{,}000$.

feedback.correct: Only normality fails, and with 2,000 days it hardly matters.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find which assumption fails, then what it is needed for.

explain.text: Only assumption 5 fails. By the central limit theorem, $\hat\beta$ is close to normal with $n = 2{,}000$ even when the errors are not. Fat tails do make single outliers more influential, so still look at the residual plot.

screens.title: Why the usual formula fails
screens.prose: Where does $\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ come from, and what replaces it under a funnel? Put the steps in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \boldsymbol\beta + (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\boldsymbol\varepsilon$: put $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon$ into the normal equations' solution

With a funnel, $\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)$ is diagonal with unequal entries; White estimates each by $e_i^2$: $(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\left(\sum e_i^2\mathbf{x}_i\mathbf{x}_i^T\right)(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}$

hints.text: Start by writing $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ in terms of the errors.
The variance of a matrix times $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ comes next.
Substitute, take the variance, then the special case, then White's replacement.

feedback.correct: The sandwich: bread $(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ on both sides, with the error variance as the filling.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ in terms of $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ first.

byKey.usual: The special case needs the general variance formula first.
byKey.white: White's estimate replaces the general middle term, so it comes last.

explain.text: Line 1 also shows unbiasedness: if the errors average zero given $\mathbf{X}$, so does $(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\boldsymbol\varepsilon$. The variance assumption enters only at line 3. HC1 multiplies White's estimate by $n/(n - k - 1)$; HAC also adds cross terms $e_te_s$ for nearby days.

screens.title: Overlapping returns
screens.prose: A backtest regresses each day's next-20-day return on its past-20-day return, over 1,000 days. Neighbouring windows share 19 days, so both series are autocorrelated by construction. In 2,000 simulations with no true effect, the naive $t$ had standard deviation 3.63, not 1.

state.caption: No true effect in any simulation

screens.question: The backtest reports a naive $t = 4.0$. Roughly what is the honest $t$?

hints.text: The naive $t$ is spread 3.63 times too widely.
Divide by that factor to put it back on the usual scale.

feedback.correct: About 1.1: no evidence of an effect.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shrink the naive $t$ by the factor 3.63.

byKey.same: You trusted the naive $t$. Under no effect it beats 1.96 in 60% of backtests.
byKey.sqrt20: You divided by $\sqrt{20} = 4.47$. The simulated factor here is 3.63.
byKey.times: You multiplied. The naive $t$ is too large, so divide.

explain.text: $4.0 / 3.63 \approx 1.1$. With no true effect, the naive $t$ clears 1.96 in 60% of backtests. HAC errors with 40 lags cut that to 11%, still above 5%; sampling every 20th day removes the overlap entirely.

ideas: A funnel (changing variance) or autocorrelation leaves $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ unbiased but makes the usual standard errors wrong, usually too small.
Check with a residual plot and the Durbin-Watson $d$ (near 2 is fine, near 0 is trouble); fix the errors with `cov_type="HC1"` or `cov_type="HAC"`.
Robust errors do not fix a wrong model, and non-overlapping returns with $d$ near 2 need no HAC correction.

formula.name: Robust (sandwich) covariance
formula.note: With constant variance it reduces to $s^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}$.

summary.trap: A $p$-value of 0.000 from daily levels or overlapping returns can be pure autocorrelation: check $d$ and use HAC errors before believing it.

quiz.prose: The residuals of a straight-line fit form a U: positive at both ends, negative in the middle. A colleague switches to HC1 standard errors.
quiz.question: Does that fix the problem?

options.text: No: robust errors fix the standard errors, not a wrong model
Yes: HC1 handles any pattern in the residuals
options.why: You treated robust errors as a cure-all. A U shape means the line is the wrong shape, so $\hat\beta$ itself is off.

options.text: No, but HAC errors would
options.why: HAC errors also leave the model unchanged. A curve needs a curved model, such as an $x^2$ term.

options.text: Only if $y$ is logged first
options.why: Logging $y$ changes the question being asked. Fit the shape the data show.

feedback.correct: A U in the residuals means the model is wrong; no standard error fixes that.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a U-shaped residual plot says about the line.

explain.text: Robust errors correct the spread of a correctly specified $\hat\beta$. A U-shaped residual plot says the mean of $y$ is curved, so the straight-line slope is the wrong target. Add the missing term first.

quiz.prose: A regression's residuals give $\sum(e_t - e_{t-1})^2 = 2.2$ and $\sum e_t^2 = 2.0$.
quiz.question: What is the Durbin-Watson statistic?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the sum of squared changes by the sum of squared residuals.

byKey.inv: You divided the wrong way up. The changes go on top.

explain.text: $d = 2.2/2.0 = 1.1$. Using $d \approx 2(1 - \hat\rho)$ gives $\hat\rho \approx 0.45$. That is enough to make the usual standard errors too small.

quiz.prose: To remove the funnel in the execution cost data, a colleague regresses $\ln(\text{cost})$ on order size instead of cost.
quiz.question: What is the main thing to understand before doing this?

options.text: The slope now answers a different question: the % change in cost per £m
Nothing: logging only fixes the variance
options.why: You treated the log as a variance fix alone. It also changes what the slope means and what the model predicts.

options.text: The slope was biased before, and the log removes the bias
options.why: The funnel never biased the slope. It only misjudged its standard error.

options.text: Logs always remove a funnel
options.why: Only when the spread grows in proportion to the level. Otherwise a new pattern appears.

feedback.correct: Logging changes the model, not just its errors.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what the new slope measures.

explain.text: In $\ln(\text{cost}) = a + b\,\text{size}$, $b$ is roughly the proportional change in cost per £m. That may be a better model, but it is a new model. If the question is about £k of cost, keep the line and use robust errors.

quiz.prose: A stock's beta regression on daily returns: residuals are independent from day to day, but their size grows on volatile market days.
quiz.question: Which standard errors should we report?

options.text: HC1 (White) robust errors
The usual ones: the residuals are independent
options.why: Independence is only half of it. Variance that changes with the market breaks the usual formula.

options.text: HAC with many lags: daily data are always autocorrelated
options.why: These residuals are independent. HAC would work but costs precision for no gain.

options.text: Drop the volatile days
options.why: Dropping data to fit an assumption throws away the days that matter most for beta.

feedback.correct: Changing variance with independent days calls for HC errors.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the fix to the assumption that fails.

explain.text: Volatility clustering makes the error variance move with the market: heteroscedasticity. With independent days, HC1 errors are the right fix. HAC errors would also be valid, just noisier.
